summary: Defines an SMTP extension in which the client estimates the message size so the server can decline it, perhaps temporarily. It was a draft standard. It was replaced by RFC 1870.

plainLanguage.summary: Before sending a big package, you tell the receiver how big it is. If it will not fit, they say no early. A newer version replaced it.

questions: what is the smtp size extension
how does smtp declare message size
subtitle: How an SMTP client can announce a message's size up front so the server can say no before the data is sent.

tldr.problem: With plain SMTP, a client only learns that a message is too big, or that the server lacks space, after sending the whole message, which the server then discards.
tldr.mechanism: Servers advertise a SIZE keyword in the EHLO reply, and clients add a SIZE parameter to the MAIL FROM command so the server can answer 452 or 552 before any data moves.
tldr.outcome: Size problems are caught early, but a 250 reply is not a guarantee. This RFC was obsoleted by RFC 1870.

today: RFC 1653 is obsolete: it was replaced by RFC 1870. It obsoleted RFC 1427 and was a Draft Standard.

sections.title: Why Declare Message Size
sections.content:
The MIME extensions let Internet mail carry many kinds of data, so SMTP is expected to carry a much wider range of message sizes than before. That affects the resources, such as disk space, that a receiving server needs.

This memo uses the SMTP service extension mechanism to let a client (the sender-SMTP) declare a message's size to a server (the receiver-SMTP). The server can then say whether it is willing to accept the message. A server can also announce the largest message it will take.

Without the extension, a client using plain SMTP only finds out about such failures after sending the entire message, and the server throws the transferred message away.
sections.plainLanguage: Without this, you carry a heavy package all the way to the door before anyone tells you it does not fit. With it, you ask first.

sections.title: The SIZE Extension Framework
sections.content:
The extension is named Message Size Declaration. Its EHLO keyword is SIZE. It adds no new SMTP verbs.

  • In the server's EHLO reply, SIZE may carry one optional parameter: a decimal number giving the fixed maximum message size in bytes that the server will accept.
  • A value of 0 means no fixed maximum is in force. If the parameter is omitted, nothing is said about a fixed maximum.
  • The MAIL FROM command gains one optional SIZE parameter: a decimal number giving the size of the message about to be sent.

A client that sees code 250 to its EHLO with the SIZE keyword knows the server supports the extension. If a numeric parameter is present, any attempt to send a larger message is rejected with the permanent failure code 552.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can put a sign on its door saying the biggest box it takes. The sender can also write the size on the delivery slip.

sections.title: The Extended MAIL Command and Replies
sections.content:
The message size counts octets, including CR-LF pairs, that the client sends after the 354 reply to DATA. The declared size should cover header, body and the CR-LF sequences between lines. Only one SIZE parameter may appear in a single MAIL command. Exact computation may be infeasible, so a client may use a heuristic estimate, and heuristics should be chosen so the declared size is usually larger than the real size. Servers MUST NOT use the SIZE value to find the end of the content in DATA.

On receiving the extended MAIL, the server checks the declared size against its fixed maximum and may check whether it has resources to hold the message. It may answer with 452 insufficient system storage if it may be able to accept the message later, or 552 if the size exceeds its fixed maximum.

After a 452, the client should send RSET or QUIT and try again later. After a 552, it should send RSET or QUIT and treat the message as undeliverable, notifying the sender if a sender address was present. A server may also return 452 or 552 in reply to a RCPT command for a particular recipient. After 452 the client may requeue for that recipient, but after 552 it may not.
sections.plainLanguage: If the answer is 'not now', you come back later. If the answer is 'never, too big', you tell the person who sent it that it cannot be delivered.

sections.title: Limits of the Promise and Minimal Use
sections.content:
A 250 reply to the extended MAIL is not an absolute guarantee. Clients must still be ready for 452 and 552 after DATA or after the transfer. A server may accept a message somewhat larger than declared, and should not return 552 after the transfer unless the actual size is greater than the declared size. A client may declare a size smaller than the real one, but then a 250 gives no assurance that the message will be accepted.

A minimal client can just compare its message size with the number in the EHLO SIZE parameter, without declaring sizes in MAIL, but then it cannot learn about temporary or per-recipient limits. A minimal server may just advertise its limit, accept the extended MAIL and return 552 when the declared size is over the limit.
sections.plainLanguage: A 'yes, bring it' is a good sign, not a promise. If you said the box was small and it was huge, they can still turn you away at the door.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC notes that the size information and the extended MAIL command could conceivably make crude denial-of-service attacks somewhat quicker and easier to devise. It adds that, unless implementations are very weak, the extension creates no vulnerability that has not always existed with SMTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling people how much you can hold might help a troublemaker plan to overload you, but they could already try that anyway.
